results.question: State the exit invariant that applies to discretionary exits.
results.answer: The invariant is that **a discretionary exit (trailing stop or strategy signal) may not close a position at a net loss**. Protective exits (stop-loss, ATR stop, break-even) are exempt, because realising a loss is their purpose. It was adopted on 2026-09-01 as an invariant rather than retuned percentages: on crypto, the 1.5 / 1.5 trailing stop against a 1.206% round trip needed a peak above 2.71% to break even but armed at 1.5%. Held-back exits are logged so that a suppressed exit can be told apart from a bot that has stopped working. results.question: What are the standing rules at the end of the decision log?
results.answer: The seven standing rules are: (1) never report a result on the data used to select it, so choose in-sample and report out-of-sample or walk forward; (2) beating buy-and-hold is the bar, not beating zero; (3) count effective trades, not pooled trades; and (4) register criteria before the run, since a mid-run change voids it. The remaining rules are: (5) "not measured" never scores as "passed"; (6) optimise per-trade Sharpe rather than net P&L, because it decides whether you can ever know; and (7) restart with `restart_bots.py`, never `pm2 restart --update-env`. results.question: What went wrong on 2026-08-27 with the crypto bots?
results.answer: On 2026-08-27, a `pm2 restart --update-env` run from a shell holding `.env` overwrote eight crypto bots' identities with `.env`'s single `TRADING_PAIR` in under a second, so all nine bots traded BTC-USDC and wrote to the same state file; the advice that caused this was documented in the repo itself. Nothing raised an error, and the only symptom was per-coin trade files that stopped growing, which looked like a quiet market. It was caught after 36 minutes, when an unrelated script asked the registry which coins were running and got `BTC-USDC` nine times; no trades were lost, but that was luck. The fix added three layers: `utils/identity.py` (bots refuse to start on a name/symbol mismatch), `registry.audit()` (drift detection surfaced on the dashboard and in the nightly email), and `restart_bots.py` as the only restart path that restates and verifies identity. results.question: How does the local candle store treat a candle that is still forming?
results.answer: The store never saves a candle that is still forming; it only appends **closed** candles. A forming candle's high, low and close are partial and get revised later, so a backtest built on one would read prices no trader could have acted on, and it would err optimistically every time. In practice, the unfinished-candle guard fires on every run and refuses exactly one forming candle per series, across the 9 pairs and 35,892 stored candles. results.question: What per-trade Sharpe was measured for stocks, and how many independent trades would a conclusive test need?
results.answer: The measured per-trade Sharpe for the stocks strategy is **0.074**, so a conclusive test would need about **700 independent trades**. results.question: Why would a high win rate on the crypto Donchian profile be a warning sign rather than good news?
results.answer: **A high win rate on this profile would most likely mean someone tightened the exits, and tighter exits are what make this rule lose money.** The Donchian rule profits from a few large winners: only about 30–50% of trades win, and the winners are several times the size of the losers, so the 1.0% round-trip fee barely matters on the trades that count. In backtest, the 80/40 rule with a 15% stop made +$128 at a 50% win rate, but adding the SIM profile's 8% take-profit raised the win rate to 60% and cut the net to +$20, because capping the winners is how this rule dies. That is why win rate is explicitly not a criterion for the sealed `2026-09-crypto-donchian-breakout` run, and why any TAKE_PROFIT or TRAILING_STOP exit in the logs means the profile was changed and the run stops.
